extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of formal logic, philosophy of science, and anyone learning symbolic methods of inference
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and operational rules for performing the Indirect Method of Inference (Boole-style symbolic logic): how to develop terms, form all alternatives, eliminate contradictions, apply contrapositives and abstractions, and use mechanical aids to reach complete logical descriptions from premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Indirect Method of Inference (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indirect Method of Inference furnishes a complete solution of the following problem—Given any number of logical premises or conditions, required the description of any class of objects, or of any term, as governed by those conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic of the Indirect process: it gives all possible logical conclusions (both those from direct substitution and many others). It operates by developing all alternatives for terms and eliminating those inconsistent with premises; examples throughout the chapter illustrate obtaining full descriptions (e.g., iron=iron, metal, element).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise steps of the Indirect Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The steps of the process of inference may thus be concisely stated:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. By the Law of Duality develop the utmost number of alternatives which may exist in the description of the required class or term as regards the terms involved in the premises. 2. For each term, in these alternatives substitute its description as given in the premises. 3. Strike out every alternative which is then found to break the Law of Contradiction. 4. The remaining terms may be equated to the term in question as the desired description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Duality / Development of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Law of Duality each term must be either positive or negative; when n terms are present develop all 2^n conceivable alternatives (e.g., for two terms AB, Ab, aB, ab; for three terms eight combinations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the 'development' of a term by listing all combinations in which it may occur, then substitute premises' descriptions into those alternatives. Example: from A=AB and B=BC derive A=ABC by eliminating contradictions after substitution. The Logical Alphabet is the prepared list of these combinations (printed up to six terms in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Contradiction — strike out inconsistent alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: After substituting descriptions of terms into the set of alternatives, strike out every alternative found to 'break the Law of Contradiction' (i.e., that contains an explicit contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining (non-contradictory) combinations constitute the valid description(s) of the term in question. Many worked examples show striking out self-contradictory combinations to derive conclusions (e.g., Barbara example leaves only ABC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Contrapositive (including contrapositive of a simple identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying Indirect Inference one may form the contrapositive of propositions (including simple identities A = B) and substitute these contrapositives into other premises to derive further results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From 'heated solids give continuous spectra' and 'some nebulae do not give continuous spectra' derive 'some nebulae are not heated solids' by forming and substituting contrapositives. For A = B one can derive not-B = not-A and also other contrapositives and combine them to obtain further equalities (illustrated in the 'Contrapositive of a Simple Identity' section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of equivalents (repeated substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a term is given an equivalent description in a premise, substitute that equivalent expression into other premises or alternatives to discover consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution may be applied repeatedly (including substituting contrapositives) to reveal hidden implications. The text shows repeatedly substituting described equivalents into alternative combinations to reduce possibilities and produce explicit descriptions such as A = ABC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction of indifferent circumstances (abstraction/elision)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two alternatives differ only by a single component term (positive in one and negative in the other), that indifferent part may be struck out and the alternatives reduced to one term: abstraction eliminates indifferent components that convey no new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From A = ABC .|. ABc we may abstract to A = AB because the differing C/c is indifferent. Caveat: some alternative pairs that look indifferent can imply real information (e.g., 'with or without three equal angles' expresses that some triangles have three equal angles). Also, one cannot in general abstract C from AC = BC to infer A = B; abstraction requires the form where the alternatives differ only in an indifferent term and identical second members to permit substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Alphabet and the representation of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a complete series of combinations (the Logical Alphabet) to represent the full development of a term of a proposition: e.g., X = XAB .|. XAb .|. XaB .|. Xah for the four combinations of two terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Logical Alphabet is printed (convenience up to six terms) and serves as the universe of alternatives for analysis. The unit class X may be understood implicitly when listing combinations. Treat every combination as part of a proposition; selecting combinations that contain a given letter produces the development of that letter (e.g., selecting A's yields AX = XAB .|. XA b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation and mechanical aids for the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical employment of the method can be simplified by devices: printed sheets with series of combinations, sheets with slits to fold down combinations, Logical Slate (combinations engraved on a slate), and the Abacus (mechanical arrangement of slips/pins) to select and strike out combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices reduce manual and mental labour and the chance of error. The author notes it's hardly possible to apply the process to problems of more than six terms owing to the large number of combinations; the slate and abacus methods are described step-by-step (e.g., lifting combinations with a flat rule to separate classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits and labour considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of combinations grows exponentially with the number of terms (4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ...), making the process laborious and error-prone for many terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the labour and chance of mistake, the author recommends mechanical aids and acknowledges that application beyond six terms becomes impracticable without such aids. The text gives techniques to lessen both manual and mental labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the method and prevention of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rules of the Indirect Method are correctly followed, the whole truth can be extracted from a series of propositions and the method prevents common fallacies and paralogisms of ordinary discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method is shown to avoid fallacies such as those arising from negative premises, the Undistributed Middle, and the Illicit Process of the Major Term; worked examples (granite/basalt, planets/fixed stars) show that the method avoids drawing unwarranted conclusions that ordinary reasoning might produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and precise symbolic formulation of premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficult or composite natural-language premises should be carefully parsed and expressed in precise symbolic forms (e.g., splitting statements about 'all metals except gold and silver are opaque' into multiple premises) before applying the Indirect Method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates translating complex statements into a set of symbolic premises (sometimes several) so that the full meaning is captured (example: metals except gold and silver requires separate premises for gold and silver being non-opaque metals and the exclusion gold≠silver). Correct symbolic formulation is essential to obtain complete and accurate conclusions.
